body.text: Jammu Kashmir Refugee Representation in AJK, State Unity, and Our Political Disorientation.

A contentious and fresh debate is currently emerging within Azad Jammu and Kashmir regarding the reserved seats and political representation of Jammu and Kashmir refugees in the Legislative Assembly. On the surface, this appears to be a mere constitutional and electoral issue; in reality, however, this question is deeply intertwined with the historical unity, geographical identity, and future political vision of the State of Jammu and Kashmir. Regrettably, instead of foresight and serious dialogue on a subject with such sensitive and far-reaching implications, emotional slogans, religious decrees (fatwas), and dangerous trends of social polarization are being promoted.

It is astonishing that the circles objecting to refugee representation are either entirely ignorant of the historical and political sensitivity of this issue, or they are deliberately erecting artificial and hateful walls of local vs. refugee to achieve their specific, short-term objectives.
Historical Context and Forced Displacement

The historical and undeniable reality is that prior to August 15, 1947, the entire State of Jammu and Kashmir including Jammu, Ladakh, the Valley, Gilgit-Baltistan, and present-day Azad Kashmir was an indivisible political and geographical entity. Following the partition of India, subsequent regional wars, and international political interests, this region was fractured into different parts. This forced partition did not merely alter the geography of the region; it plunged millions of human beings into displacement from their centuries-old homeland, separation from their loved ones, economic deprivation, and above all, a permanent crisis of identity.
The refugees of Jammu and Kashmir are not the byproduct of a specific era or a single event; rather, multiple bloody and political tragedies have driven their displacement.

The Tragedy of 1947: At the time of Partition, hundreds of thousands of Kashmiris from Jammu and other areas were forced to migrate through organized violence, taking refuge in various districts of Pakistan and Azad Kashmir.

The 1965 and 1971 Wars: As a result of the Indo-Pak wars, new migrations emerged from areas close to the Working Boundary and the Ceasefire Line, particularly from the Poonch, Chhamb, and Jammu sectors.

The 1989 Armed Conflict: Following the armed movement that erupted in the Kashmir Valley and the subsequent state oppression, thousands of families crossed the Line of Control to take refuge in the camps of Azad Kashmir. The bitter truth is that this security and political crisis has not ceased even today.
Displacement does not erase identity, nor does it strip citizens of their political rights.
Constitutional Foundations of Refugee Representation

An unassailable question of principle arises here: does any citizen forced to relocate within their own state due to the compulsion of circumstances lose their fundamental state identity and political right to franchise? If, under United Nations resolutions and international law, the State of Jammu and Kashmir remains a disputed and undecided entity, then every single one of its citizens no matter which corner of the world or which city of Pakistan they reside in must possess the full right to representation and freedom of expression within the state's political system.

An examination of Azad Kashmir's constitutional framework reveals that the Azad Jammu and Kashmir Act of 1970, and the subsequently framed Interim Constitution of 1974, reserved 12 seats in constituencies spread across Pakistan. The primary objective was to ensure that until a final decision regarding the entire state is reached, the Kashmiri refugees residing in Pakistan remain connected to the statehood and assembly of Jammu and Kashmir. To abolish these seats or to oppose them is practically tantamount to accepting this partition as a permanent reality.
Abolishing refugee seats is equivalent to accepting the permanent division of Jammu and Kashmir.

We believe that the number of seats for the refugees of Jammu and Kashmir should be proportionate to the population ratios prevalent in the constituencies of Azad Kashmir, which would be a just and democratic process. The demand to abolish refugee seats directly conflicts with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and international laws governing fundamental human rights.
A Dangerous Blueprint for Division

This demand to deprive citizens holding State Subject status of their representation in the Azad Kashmir Assembly, and to abolish their acquired rights, is actually part of a covert and dangerous blueprint for the permanent division of Jammu and Kashmir. Under this plan, the objective is to divide the people of Jammu and Kashmir on religious, regional, linguistic, tribal, and political lines, erecting such mountains of hatred and animosity between them that they reach a point where the very concept of living together becomes unimaginable.

We consider all State Subject holders of the State of Jammu and Kashmir, without any discrimination of color, race, religion, creed, language, region, tribe, gender, or ideology, as equal citizens and the collective inheritors of the historic State of Jammu and Kashmir.
Economic Realities and Overseas Kashmiris

The population of Azad Kashmir is approximately 4.5 million. Due to the lack of industries and the absence of alternative livelihood options in the region, roughly forty percent of the total population is compelled to work abroad. These expatriate Kashmiris are the backbone of their families and relatives back home, providing financial assistance to maintain their vital lifelong bonds with the homeland.

Those circles that oppose the seats and quotas of Jammu and Kashmir refugees today could very well build a similar narrative against overseas Kashmiris tomorrow, arguing that because their second and third generations have permanently settled abroad, they too should be deprived of the right to vote and stripped of their right to hold property in Azad Kashmir.
Refugee representation is not a burden; it is a symbol of the State’s historical unity.
Political Manipulation and Structural Issues

Blaming the refugees entirely for the current political, economic, and administrative issues of Azad Kashmir is not only a historical injustice but also gross political dishonesty. The fundamental issues stem primarily from Pakistan's federal policies, the ambiguous power structure between Islamabad and Muzaffarabad, and the incompetence of the local ruling elite.

Truth be told, for the past three-quarters of a century, this entire region has been held hostage by the two major state narratives of South Asia, the politics of power hegemony, and the deceptive maneuvers of the local ruling classes. The heaviest price of this tug-of-war has always been paid by the ordinary Kashmiri.
Threats to Democratic Stability

There appears to be a plot to delay the general elections expected in Azad Kashmir this July. Certain elements wish to instigate bloodshed and anarchy. Under such circumstances, wisdom demands vigilance. If conditions deteriorate drastically, it is possible that the entire political and constitutional system could be wrapped up altogether.

If conditions reach a critical precipice where this system is dismantled and a retired military officer, judge, or bureaucrat is installed as a custodian, where will the public go then? To whom will they turn for justice?
Peaceful struggle, negotiation, and unity are the only vehicles that can lead us to our true destination.
The Fundamental Question

The fundamental and paramount question remains: how do the people of the State of Jammu and Kashmir steer the issue of their political future, their usurped identity, and their right to self-determination toward a just, democratic, and sustainable solution? Until we achieve absolute clarity and consensus on this strategic question and forge unity within our ranks, this region will continue to languish in internal strife, uncertainty, forced displacements, and political disorientation.

Sardar Shaukat Ali Kashmiri, Chairman of the United Kashmir People's Party, is a secular, progressive Kashmiri politician and renowned human rights defender. Originally from Trarkhel Sudhanoti, Azad Kashmir, he is currently based in Switzerland.
